question: Which properties of a scientific problem, its data, and its deployment setting should make a researcher avoid machine learning or sharply limit the claims made from it?

key_findings.claim: The paper offers a useful preflight checklist centered on identifiability, signal, support coverage, prior knowledge, and deployment validation rather than on choosing a fashionable model.
key_findings.evidence: Its recurring decision rule is to ask whether the available representation distinguishes targets, whether the desired relation is learnable from available information, whether training and deployment data overlap in the relevant ways, and whether performance in the actual use case can be verified. If not, the author recommends reformulating the problem, collecting more informative data, adding justified prior structure, or using a different technique.

anchors.section: II The devil's in the distance
Inverse problems, signal-to-noise, and Section III

key_findings.claim: The distinction between an untouched test set and a deployment-representative test is the paper's strongest practical point.
key_findings.evidence: A holdout can be disjoint from training and validation yet still overlap the training distribution much more than the eventual deployment distribution. Figure 2 makes this visually explicit, and the text uses simulation-to-experiment transfer as a scientific example. The paper therefore requires both pipeline independence and relevance to the use case, and says an unverifiable deployment model should not be used.

anchors.section: III On the importance of data distributions

key_findings.claim: Keeping the final test set untouched is necessary but does not make 'any' remaining tuning procedure appropriate, contrary to the paper's wording.
key_findings.evidence: Page 4 says that as long as the test set is not used during development, any approach to model tuning is appropriate. This omits leakage through preprocessing, entity or temporal overlap, feature construction, label availability, non-nested model selection, duplicated samples, and target-derived data curation. It also omits underspecification: many predictors can tie on in-distribution validation and diverge in deployment even without test contamination. Contemporary primary studies document these failures across hundreds of scientific papers and multiple application domains.

anchors.section: Start of Section III and Footnote 3

key_findings.claim: The claim that machine learning can only model functions with one unique output per input is technically false and makes the inverse-problem exclusion too broad.
key_findings.evidence: The paper treats non-unique inverse maps as unsuitable until restricted to a non-degenerate functional subspace. Point predictors do collapse ambiguity, but probabilistic supervised models learn conditional distributions, latent-variable and invertible models represent multiple solutions, and posterior samplers explicitly target p(x|y). Diffusion posterior sampling now handles noisy nonlinear inverse problems including the paper's own phase-retrieval example. Non-identifiability remains and must appear as posterior uncertainty, but it does not preclude machine learning.

key_findings.claim: Distance is a helpful pedagogical lens but not a universal foundation for supervised machine learning in the sense asserted.
key_findings.evidence: The paper groups norms, divergences, cross-entropy, reinforcement learning, clustering, autoencoders, random forests, and numerical optimization under distance. Empirical-risk methods do optimize losses, but cross-entropy is not a metric, input-space proximity is representation- and model-dependent, trees partition coordinates without a global distance, and conditional likelihood methods need not encode semantic similarity as Euclidean proximity. The useful invariant is loss plus inductive bias plus sampling assumptions, not distance alone.

key_findings.claim: The information-and-prior argument is sound in spirit, but the categorical statement that data-driven models do not extrapolate is too strong.
key_findings.evidence: The paper correctly argues that behavior outside observed support is selected by inductive bias rather than certified by training fit. Yet extrapolation is task-, representation-, architecture-, and distribution-dependent: structured models can extrapolate linear rules, algorithms, symmetries, periodic structure, or causal mechanisms when the appropriate bias is learned or encoded. Primary theory identifies conditions under which MLPs and graph networks do and do not extrapolate, so the defensible claim is that unsupported extrapolation lacks a guarantee, not that it never occurs.

anchors.section: IV The data-driven 'no free lunch theorem'

key_findings.claim: The section titled a data-driven 'no free lunch theorem' presents an intuition about inductive bias, not the formal supervised-learning no-free-lunch theorem.
key_findings.evidence: No theorem, assumptions, loss, task distribution, or proof is stated. Formal no-free-lunch results average uniformly over all target problems or otherwise quantify a specified problem family; they do not imply that every learner fails to extrapolate on structured real-world distributions. Later work emphasizes that real data are strongly non-uniform and low-complexity, precisely why reusable architectural biases can outperform uniform-problem conclusions.

anchors.section: IV The data-driven 'no free lunch theorem'

key_findings.claim: Figure 3 is a didactic illustration of inductive bias, not evidence that Gaussian processes generally extrapolate better than neural networks.
key_findings.evidence: A periodic-kernel Gaussian process is given the correct qualitative form for sin(4x), while an unspecified neural network receives no periodic encoding and only minimizes MSE. The paper reports neither architecture, optimizer, initialization, training steps, kernel fitting details, sample coordinates, error metric, repeated seeds, nor code. Its statement that no amount of wider-range data can teach a neural model periodicity is also categorical; periodic features or suitable architectures change the result. The figure demonstrates that the right prior can dominate sparse data, not a model-class ranking.

key_findings.claim: The Bayesian claim that a model reverts to 'the mean' away from data is only true for the specific zero-mean local-kernel example, not for Bayesian models in general.
key_findings.evidence: A posterior predictive tends toward its prior predictive only where observations cease to inform the relevant latent variables and parameters. That prior can have a nonzero trend, periodic structure, heavy tails, hierarchical coupling, or globally updated parameters; it need not be a constant mean. Figure 3 uses a zero-mean Gaussian-process prior, so the observed return toward zero cannot justify the universal statement made in the prose.

key_findings.claim: The recommended uncertainty quantification and active-learning loop is directionally useful but is not itself a reliability certificate under shift.
key_findings.evidence: The paper suggests Gaussian processes and ensembles because their uncertainty can guide sampling where the system is likely out of sample. Large-scale primary evaluations show that uncertainty calibration often deteriorates with dataset shift, although model-marginalizing methods can be stronger, and shift detectors can detect benign and harmful shifts alike. Active learning can expand sampled support only when its acquisition score recognizes ignorance and an oracle can supply reliable labels or experiments.

key_findings.claim: The perspective contains no systematic evidence that its proposed stop conditions predict project success or failure.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 is one synthetic Gaussian-process fit, Figure 2 is a conceptual overlap diagram, and Figure 3 is one underspecified toy comparison. The materials examples are literature anecdotes rather than a sampled audit. There is no decision rubric with thresholds, retrospective project cohort, prospective validation, ablation, sensitivity analysis, cost model, error bars, or comparison to alternative readiness frameworks.

method.core_idea: Use an information-first qualitative audit to decide whether machine learning is appropriate before spending effort on architecture selection or training.
method.mechanism: The perspective reduces supervised learning to fitting a relation under a loss, then asks whether the chosen representation and available data contain discriminative signal at the target's relevant length scales. It screens inverse problems for identifiability and signal-to-noise, separates holdout independence from deployment representativeness, and treats training support plus prior structure as the boundary of defensible prediction. Three didactic examples illustrate multiscale fitting, train-test-deploy distribution mismatch, and the effect of a periodic prior. When deployment can move beyond support, the paper proposes uncertainty estimation and active learning; when performance cannot be verified, it recommends not using the model.
assumptions: The primary target is supervised scientific prediction, even though conclusions are sometimes generalized to all data-driven methods.
Input and output representations expose task-relevant distinctions rather than nuisance variation.
The target relation is sufficiently stable and smooth at the sampling resolution for finite-data learning.
Signal-to-noise and identifiability can be assessed before or during modeling.
A disjoint test set can be held untouched until the pipeline is finalized.
The deployment population can be specified well enough to judge whether a test set represents it.
Labeled or otherwise trustworthy deployment data can be acquired when direct validation is required.
Distribution similarity in the observed representation tracks similarity of the conditional prediction problem.
Prior structure is scientifically justified rather than selected after observing test failures.
Uncertainty estimates rise when inputs leave the model's supported information region.
An active-learning oracle can return sufficiently accurate labels or experimental outcomes at acceptable cost.
The toy Gaussian-process and neural-network behavior transfers qualitatively to high-dimensional scientific systems.
A point-function view adequately represents the intended prediction task; this assumption excludes distributional inverse solutions.
Human judgment can identify use cases and failure modes that the learned system cannot reliably detect itself.

techniques.role: Screens data availability, identifiability, support, deployment, and validation before model construction.
Compares feature distinctions with target distinctions to detect inadequate encodings.
Asks whether target alternatives remain resolvable given measurement noise.
Keeps final evaluation data outside training, preprocessing decisions, and hyperparameter selection.
Separates in-distribution test performance from performance on the actual deployment population.
Constrains unsupported behavior with known functional form, correlations, symmetries, or boundaries.
Uses radial-basis and periodic Gaussian-process kernels to illustrate length scale and prior effects.
Attaches predictive uncertainty to ambiguous inversions and possible out-of-support inputs.
Queries new labels or experiments in uncertain regions to expand the supported interpolation window.
Retains scientific hypothesis formation, use-case selection, and go/no-go authority with researchers.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic multiscale one-dimensional function F(x)=5x^2+sin(50x)/3 plus Gaussian noise
evaluations.metric: Visual fit of a radial-basis-function Gaussian process to broad trend and small oscillations
evaluations.result: Figure 1 captures the broad quadratic trend but not the sparse high-frequency oscillations; no numerical error, kernel-selection procedure, repeated draw, code, or baseline is reported.
evaluations.baseline: No fitted comparator; the caption only notes that a more sophisticated non-isotropic kernel could model both scales if supplied with sufficient prior information

evaluations.result: Figure 2 shows a disjoint test sample overlapping the training distribution while deployment only partly overlaps both, illustrating why standard held-out performance can overstate deployment validity; it contains no measured data.
evaluations.baseline: The conventional assumption that an untouched same-source holdout is sufficient evidence for deployment

evaluations.metric: Visual interpolation and extrapolation of an unspecified neural network and a periodic-kernel Gaussian process
evaluations.result: Both follow observed clusters, while the neural network behaves irregularly in gaps and outside them and the Gaussian process continues a periodic pattern before reverting toward its zero prior mean. No architecture, training setup, sample values, quantitative metric, variance over seeds, or code is given.
evaluations.baseline: A generic MSE-trained neural network without stated periodic features versus a Gaussian process given the correct periodic inductive bias

evaluations.setting: Narrative materials-science cases involving simulated-to-experimental transfer, neural-network potentials, diffraction, and spectroscopy
evaluations.metric: Consistency with selected cited successes and failures
evaluations.result: The examples motivate narrow-domain utility and distribution mismatch, but the article performs no reanalysis, systematic sampling, or outcome prediction across projects.
evaluations.baseline: Selected prior publications rather than a controlled readiness framework or empirical project cohort

evaluations.metric: Validation of proposed ML go/no-go criteria against observed project outcomes
evaluations.result: No such validation is provided; the article is a seven-page perspective with three illustrations and a qualitative synthesis.
evaluations.baseline: Later primary work providing multi-domain shift benchmarks, leakage taxonomies, uncertainty comparisons, deployment filters, and inverse-problem experiments

limitations: The article is a perspective, not a theorem, systematic review, benchmark, or validated decision instrument.
Its broad definition of distance conflates loss functions, input geometry, representation similarity, and optimization.
The unique-output function requirement excludes conditional-density, Bayesian, generative, set-valued, and posterior-sampling predictors.
Low signal-to-noise is treated qualitatively; no information, utility, sample-size, or experimental-cost threshold defines when ML becomes inappropriate.
Untouched-test guidance omits many leakage paths and says too broadly that any other tuning procedure is appropriate.
Deployment representativeness is advocated but not operationally defined for temporal drift, rare events, feedback loops, or multiple user populations.
The article does not distinguish covariate shift, label shift, concept shift, subpopulation shift, and measurement-process shift.
The extrapolation claim is categorical despite known task-dependent successes with suitable architecture, features, priors, and adaptation.
The 'no free lunch theorem' label does not state the formal theorem's averaging assumptions and can mislead readers about structured real-world tasks.
The Gaussian-process demonstrations are not reproducible from the article because data, code, hyperparameters, and fitting details are absent.
Figure 3 privileges one model with the correct periodic kernel, so it cannot compare model families fairly.
The Bayesian reversion claim mistakes a zero-mean Gaussian-process special case for a property of all Bayesian predictive models.
Uncertainty and active learning are proposed without auditing calibration failure, acquisition bias, oracle errors, or labeling cost.
Human oversight is endorsed rhetorically but no responsibility allocation, escalation rule, documentation protocol, or human-factors evaluation is supplied.
The article's claims about sentient AI, human-brain complexity, and future AI winters are unsupported speculation outside its evidence.
failure_modes: A same-source random split leaks entities, time, sites, preprocessing statistics, or future information while still appearing untouched.
An in-distribution holdout gives excellent scores but omits the hospitals, instruments, materials, operating regimes, or users encountered after deployment.
A representation merges physically distinct states, making the inverse target non-identifiable even for a powerful predictor.
A point estimate hides a multimodal inverse posterior and is mistaken for a uniquely recovered scientific state.
A model's confidence remains high under shift, so uncertainty sampling never queries the region where it is wrong.
A generic domain classifier detects a harmless covariate shift but cannot tell that performance is stable, causing unnecessary rejection.
A shift detector sees both benign and catastrophic changes equally and is mistaken for a performance monitor.
A carefully chosen prior overwhelms sparse data but encodes the wrong symmetry or boundary behavior, producing confident systematic error.
Repeated validation tuning overfits the validation set despite a formally untouched final test, and a single final score hides selection instability.
Multiple equally accurate in-domain models exploit different shortcuts and diverge after deployment because the pipeline is underspecified.
Active learning queries high-uncertainty but low-value or unreachable points, exhausting experiment budget without improving deployment risk.
Simulation-trained models inherit simulator bias that is invisible on synthetic holdouts and only appears on experimental measurements.
A neural network is declared incapable of extrapolation based on one unspecified seed and architecture even though the relevant structure could be encoded or learned.
A Bayesian model's return to its prior is interpreted as calibrated ignorance even though the prior itself is misspecified.
A broad 'do not use ML' decision discards a useful probabilistic or hybrid physics-ML method because the audit assumes only deterministic point prediction.
reusable_insights: Separate four gates explicitly: information adequacy, estimator adequacy, evaluation validity, and deployment utility.
Test independence and test representativeness are orthogonal properties and should be recorded separately in every experiment card.
For inverse problems, replace a binary function test with an identifiability audit that decides whether the output should be a point, set, distribution, or abstention.
Specify distribution shifts by mechanism and anticipated consequence rather than using one undifferentiated out-of-distribution label.
A train-versus-deploy discriminator is a useful shift alarm, but pair it with a performance or decision-utility estimate before declaring the shift harmful.
Treat uncertainty calibration under each realistic shift as an evaluation target, not an assumed property of Gaussian processes, ensembles, or conformal methods.
Document every source of prior structure and test it under deliberate prior misspecification.
Use toy figures only to explain mechanisms; do not promote them to model-class conclusions without code, multiple seeds, metrics, and matched inductive biases.
Define extrapolation relative to a precise support, intervention, scale, or compositional rule; interpolation-versus-extrapolation is representation-dependent.
A practical ML readiness score should include value of information and the cost and latency of collecting deployment labels.
Benchmark simple statistical or mechanistic baselines before complex ML, because leakage and shortcut learning can manufacture apparent complexity gains.
When deployment labels are scarce, combine prospective monitoring, unlabeled shift diagnostics, small sentinel label sets, and conservative abstention rather than assuming validation is impossible.
Report the distribution of outcomes across seeds and near-optimal models to expose underspecification hidden by a single mean score.
Preserve a human-readable causal story for why the chosen features should remain predictive under the named deployment shifts.
Make the go/no-go decision falsifiable by writing explicit acceptance thresholds and failure triggers before inspecting final test results.
open_questions: Can a prospective multi-domain study validate which preflight criteria actually predict whether a scientific ML project delivers net value?
How should information adequacy be quantified for multimodal inverse posteriors without collapsing them to a misleading signal-to-noise scalar?
What minimum sentinel-label budget is needed to validate performance under a family of plausible deployment shifts?
Can unlabeled suitability signals reliably bound harmful degradation beyond classifiers and covariate shift?
How can shift detection distinguish benign, correctable, and catastrophic changes before ground-truth outcomes arrive?
Which uncertainty methods remain calibrated under combined covariate, label, and concept shift in scientific instruments?
How should active learning account jointly for epistemic uncertainty, experiment cost, safety constraints, and downstream scientific utility?
Can causal or invariant representations justify extrapolation across mechanisms more reliably than support-overlap heuristics?
What stress tests expose near-optimal models that share validation accuracy but rely on different scientific shortcuts?
How should a readiness rubric credit hybrid mechanistic-probabilistic models that remain useful even when a unique inverse is impossible?
Can formal no-free-lunch assumptions be translated into a practitioner-facing diagnostic without overstating impossibility on structured domains?
What evidence is sufficient to authorize deployment when the rare failure events of interest cannot be represented in an ordinary held-out test?
How should deployment feedback loops be modeled when predictions alter the future data distribution being monitored?
Can a reproducible version of Figures 1 and 3 map model failure against sample spacing, noise, prior mismatch, architecture, and seed?
How should human oversight be evaluated as part of the system rather than invoked as an unmeasured final safeguard?

competitive_landscape.title: Underspecification Presents Challenges for Credibility in Modern Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Same-year primary study of deployment failure despite strong in-distribution validation.
competitive_landscape.difference: D'Amour and coauthors show empirically across vision, medical imaging, NLP, clinical risk, and genomics that many predictors can tie on held-out data yet behave differently in deployment. This is a distinct and better-validated failure mode than Carbone's train-versus-deploy distribution mismatch and shows that representative splitting alone is not sufficient.

competitive_landscape.title: Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science
competitive_landscape.relationship: Same-year evidence-driven audit of methodological reasons scientific ML results fail.
competitive_landscape.difference: Kapoor and Narayanan survey 17 fields and 329 affected papers, define eight leakage types, reproduce a prediction literature, and propose model info sheets. Carbone gives general holdout advice but no leakage taxonomy, sampled evidence, or reporting protocol.

competitive_landscape.title: Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct empirical test of the uncertainty methods Carbone recommends for out-of-sample deployment.
competitive_landscape.difference: Ovadia and coauthors benchmark accuracy and calibration under multiple shifts and find that post-hoc calibration and several Bayesian approximations degrade, while model-marginalizing methods are stronger. Carbone treats uncertainty more generically and supplies no shift-calibration evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Failing Loudly: An Empirical Study of Methods for Detecting Dataset Shift
competitive_landscape.relationship: Operational predecessor for detecting the train-deploy mismatch shown conceptually in Carbone's Figure 2.
competitive_landscape.difference: Rabanser and coauthors systematically compare shift detectors and find two-sample tests on classifier representations effective, while also separating shift detection and malignancy. Carbone proposes an informal ability-to-tell-datasets-apart sanity check without a statistical test or benchmark.

competitive_landscape.title: WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts
competitive_landscape.relationship: Large multi-domain benchmark for the deployment-distribution risk at the center of the perspective.
competitive_landscape.difference: WILDS supplies ten curated real-world shifts, standardized splits, code, baselines, and persistent in-versus-out-of-distribution gaps across hospitals, cameras, time, and location. Carbone supplies a conceptual diagram and selected materials anecdotes rather than a benchmark.

competitive_landscape.title: The Effect of Natural Distribution Shift on Question Answering Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Quantitative natural-shift study that tests both holdout reuse and cross-domain deployment performance.
competitive_landscape.difference: Miller and coauthors find no adaptive overfitting on a refreshed same-domain test but measure average losses of 3.8, 14.0, and 17.4 F1 on three shifted domains, with a robust human baseline. This empirically separates test independence from deployment shift in the way Carbone argues qualitatively.

competitive_landscape.title: How Neural Networks Extrapolate: From Feedforward to Graph Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct theoretical and empirical qualification of the perspective's categorical non-extrapolation claim.
competitive_landscape.difference: Xu and coauthors prove ReLU MLPs become linear along rays, show when they can extrapolate linear targets, and link GNN extrapolation to task-specific nonlinearities encoded in architectures or features. Carbone offers one periodic toy and a blanket information-boundary statement without conditions.

competitive_landscape.title: Diffusion Posterior Sampling for General Noisy Inverse Problems
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct counterexample to excluding non-unique inverse problems from machine learning.
competitive_landscape.difference: Chung and coauthors use a learned generative prior to approximate posterior samples for noisy linear and nonlinear inverse problems, including Fourier phase retrieval and non-uniform deblurring. The method does not make an ill-posed inverse unique; it represents uncertainty over plausible solutions, which Carbone's point-function framing omits.

competitive_landscape.title: The No Free Lunch Theorem, Kolmogorov Complexity, and the Role of Inductive Biases in Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Formal correction and refinement of the no-free-lunch intuition used by the perspective.
competitive_landscape.difference: Goldblum and coauthors state the uniform-over-problems theorem, contrast it with low-complexity real data, and empirically study transferable architectural preferences. Carbone borrows the name for an informal extrapolation warning without the theorem's assumptions or the structured-data qualification.

competitive_landscape.title: Suitability Filter: A Statistical Framework for Classifier Evaluation in Real-World Deployment Settings
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later operational framework for deciding whether downstream unlabeled data remain suitable for deployment.
competitive_landscape.difference: Pouget and coauthors test whether degradation on unlabeled user data exceeds a prespecified margin using model-output suitability signals and statistical hypothesis tests. This partially relaxes Carbone's assertion that sufficient labeled deployment data must always be available, while remaining limited to detectable covariate-linked degradation.

competitive_landscape.title: Diagnosing Conformal Prediction Failures Under Distribution Shift: A COVID-19 Case Study
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current evidence that shift detection alone is insufficient and reliability diagnostics can be architecture-specific.
competitive_landscape.difference: Lee shows identical temporal shifts can yield negligible through catastrophic conformal-coverage loss, while standard shift detectors flag them uniformly; a feature-concentration diagnostic transfers partially for gradient-boosted models but misses neural-network failure modes. This supplies the nuanced, failure-severity validation missing from Carbone's distribution-overlap heuristic.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The perspective claims that understanding when not to use data-driven methods is underexplored and offers scientists a foundational account of the data conditions, pitfalls, and boundaries that determine when machine learning is appropriate.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Sections II-IV organize the argument around representation and target distances, inverse-problem identifiability and signal, train-test-deploy distributions, priors, extrapolation, uncertainty, and active learning; Section V translates these into a human-centered warning against hype and unverified use.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The article's accessible, materials-science-facing synthesis and its crisp distinction between an untouched holdout and a deployment-representative test are useful. It does not introduce a new theorem, algorithm, evidence base, or validated go/no-go rubric, and substantial primary literature already operationalized distribution shift, uncertainty failure, underspecification, and leakage. Several universal claims are technically incorrect or too broad: ML need not produce a unique point function, losses are not all distances, Bayesian models do not generically revert to a constant mean, formal no-free-lunch assumptions are omitted, and extrapolation is conditional rather than impossible. Its durable contribution is practitioner framing, not foundational ML theory.

reviewer_notes: Read all seven pages of the exact cached arXiv v1 PDF and visually inspected rendered pages 1-7 at full-page resolution, including all three figures, captions, footnotes, equations, and the complete two-page reference list. Figure 1 is a synthetic RBF-Gaussian-process illustration; Figure 2 is purely conceptual; Figure 3 is an unspecified neural-network versus periodic-kernel-GP toy. The arXiv source has one revision, submitted 2022-10-06. The version of record appeared in MRS Bulletin 47, 968-974 on 2022-10-21, DOI 10.1557/s43577-022-00417-z; claims here remain anchored to the exact hashed arXiv pages. Competitor research used current primary arXiv, JMLR, NeurIPS, and PMLR records checked through 2026-08-23, including a UAI 2026 study published during the week of this audit. The competitive panel deliberately includes direct same-year work on underspecification and scientific leakage, later posterior-sampling evidence against the unique-function claim, a formal no-free-lunch treatment, and 2025-2026 deployment diagnostics. No code or dataset accompanies the three illustrations in the paper, so their numerical behavior could not be independently reproduced from the source.
